deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is a 1953 draft on 'Fonctions de Weyl', a continuous, rearrangement-invariant version of Weyl's eigenvalue inequalities (Weyl 1949, Pólya 1950). It is the preparatory material behind Grothendieck's Séminaire Bourbaki exposé 113 (1955), 'Réarrangements de fonctions et inégalités de convexité dans les algèbres de von Neumann munies d'une trace', and behind his use of Weyl's inequalities in the Fredholm theory of nuclear operators.

Setting: I = ]0,ω[ with 0<ω≤+∞. For a measurable f, φ_f denotes its decreasing rearrangement. A 'Pólya function' (previous page, called 'fonction de Weyl' there before the renaming) is a functional P on L^∞(I), or on K^∞(I) (bounded functions with compact support), with three properties:
- (P1) P is symmetric, i.e. rearrangement invariant: P(f) depends only on φ_f.
- (P2) P is convex.
- (P3) P is lower semicontinuous for convergence in measure on each compact K. The previous page shows this is equivalent to weak* l.s.c. on L^∞(K), via Banach–Dieudonné.

This page:
(i) Localization. A function on L^∞(]0,+∞[) is a Pólya function iff each of its restrictions to L^∞(]0,ω[), 0<ω<∞, is one. A long crossed-out passage tries to formulate the converse extension statement and abandons it.
(ii) New definition. A 'Weyl function' on the positive cone L^{∞+}(]0,ω[) satisfies (P1), (P3) and (W1): f ↦ P(exp f) is a Pólya function on L^∞(]0,ω[). In other words W is convex in log f, i.e. 'geometrically convex'. On ]0,+∞[ the definition is again made by restriction to finite ω.
(iii) Representation. Since W∘exp is a symmetric convex l.s.c. functional, Fenchel–Moreau duality combined with the Hardy–Littlewood rearrangement inequality (sup over rearrangements of ∫hg equals ∫h* g*) gives W(exp f) = sup_i (a_i + ∫_0^ω φ_i φ_f), with φ_i decreasing integrable functions. Using φ_{log g} = log φ_g, it follows that W(g) = sup_i (a_i + ∫ φ_i log φ_g) for positive g with ess inf g > 0, so that log g ∈ L^∞. Hence the family (a_i, φ_i) determines W on such g, and by the l.s.c./extension argument, W entirely. The last lines (partly illegible) begin to discuss monotone (croissante) Weyl functions and their extension to the whole positive cone, continued on the next page.

Margin: example of a Pólya function, P(f) = ∫_{]0,∞[} α(f) with α convex (machine reads 'croissante'), α(0)=0, values +∞ allowed. The next page gives the Weyl analogue: W_α(f) = ∫α(f) with α(e^s) convex in s, in particular ∫|f|^p for 0<p<∞.

Purpose: an abstract framework in which Weyl–Pólya–Horn type inequalities (log-majorization implies ∫α(f) ≤ ∫α(g) for α(e^s) convex) hold for all such W. It is meant for eigenvalue versus singular-value estimates, in ℓ^p-type spaces and in traced von Neumann algebras.
errors: Second displayed formula: the upper limit is written ∞ while the first uses ω; the left-hand side should be W(f) (P(g)), not P(f). These are notational slips.
The representation needs the φ_i to be decreasing, nonnegative and integrable (paired with L^∞). This is not stated on the page.

On ]0,+∞[ the condition inf f > 0 is incompatible with compact support or integrability. The formula really only makes sense on finite ω, which is presumably why the definition proceeds by restriction.
'Détermine donc W entièrement' needs an approximation argument: from ess inf > 0 functions to general positive f, using l.s.c. or monotonicity. The page does not supply it.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a working draft of material Grothendieck published in Séminaire Bourbaki exp. 113 (1955) and used in his Fredholm theory. The abstract 'Weyl function' notion (log-majorization-monotone functionals) and its dual representation are natural and standard in later majorization and noncommutative rearrangement theory (Fack–Kosaki). It shows his early continuous, trace-based formulation, but no evidently unpublished or uncredited result.
transcription_corrections: Margin: the property of α in the example is more likely 'convexe' than 'croissante' (a Pólya function needs α convex); reading uncertain.
Second formula: the left side is better read as W(f) in context; the integral should be ∫_0^ω, not ∫_0^∞.
In the Weyl-function definition the inserted phrase read as 'continue pour L normale' is uncertain; it may be a remark on continuity or monotonicity ('croissante').
The final lines plausibly read 'La restriction d'une fonction de Weyl croissante ... est croissante. Une fonction de Pólya sur la [partie positive ...]', continuing on the next page.
